extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Christian apologetics, theology, and philosophy (general educated public, clergy, and scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and states criteria Pascal gives for recognizing, defending, and living the Christian religion — e.g., what counts as proof, what theological balances must be maintained, and what spiritual dispositions are proper. Focuses on apologetic standards (prophecy, miracle, typology), doctrinal balance (God + human misery + Redeemer), and practical/spiritual norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two fundamental points of the Christian religion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Christian religion consists in two points: (1) there is a God whom men can know, and (2) there is a corruption in their nature which renders them unworthy of Him. It is equally important to know both, and equally dangerous to know only one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal insists these two truths must be presented together because knowledge of only God without knowledge of our wretchedness produces pride, while knowledge of our wretchedness without the Redeemer produces despair. Any sound apologetic or moral teaching should therefore make both plain and balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Jesus Christ as Mediator for true knowledge of God
rubrics_metrics.description: We know God only by Jesus Christ; without this mediator all communion with God is taken away. Knowledge of God obtained without Jesus Christ is 'useless and barren'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal rejects purely metaphysical or natural proofs of God as insufficient for salvation. The presence of prophecies and the person of Christ are treated as central evidences that must be accounted for in any defense of the faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecies as mixed evidence (clear and obscure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecies are presented so that in many passages the spiritual meaning is concealed under a temporal (carnal) meaning, while in a few places the spiritual meaning is clearly revealed; some prophecies are unequivocal and some equivocal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This design makes prophecies both a proof and a test: enough clearness to convict or condemn, enough obscurity to humble and to distinguish the elect from the reprobate. A robust apologetic explains why prophecies are both hidden and revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology and the choice of the Jewish people as custodians
rubrics_metrics.description: To give faith to the Messiah, God entrusted prophecies to a carnal people (the Jews), who were above suspicion and zealous about preserving their books; their custodianship and their rejection of Christ serve as evidence of authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An argument from typology: prophetic books being in the charge of those least likely to fabricate the spiritual meaning strengthens their credibility. Explaining this prudence of God is part of apologetic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of prophetic fulfilment (time and manner)
rubrics_metrics.description: The time of prophecies is clearly foretold while the manner is often obscure; this mixture was intentional to secure both credibility and a test of disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apologetic accounts should show that exactness in timing combined with obscurity in manner aligns with the observed historical record and serves theological purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles and prophecies provide evidence yet leave room for grace
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophecies, miracles, and proofs of religion are not absolutely convincing to all, but are sufficient to make it unreasonable to reject them; they produce evidence that can enlighten some and confuse others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal frames this as intentional: evidence surpasses or equals the contrary, so refusal is ascribed to lust or malice rather than pure reason. Apologetics should therefore acknowledge limits of rational persuasion and the role of moral disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: God hides Himself and blinds or enlightens according to His will
rubrics_metrics.description: God has willed to blind some and enlighten others; there is sufficient obscurity to humble the elect and sufficient clearness to condemn the reprobate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theology and apologetics should account for the selective efficacy of evidence — why similar evidence produces different spiritual outcomes — by appealing to divine providence and human disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections from Scriptural obscurities do not destroy faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Though Scripture contains passages not clearly dictated by the Holy Spirit (or that seem contradictory), these do not harm faith; canonical and heretical writings serve to prove the canonical, and alleged obscurities are compatible with faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to objections requires showing that ambiguities are consistent with the larger design of Scripture (some things hidden, some revealed) and do not negate the core truths of the faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance: always state the contrary reason
rubrics_metrics.description: We must begin with the two contrary reasons and even add at the end of each truth that the opposite truth is to be remembered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal recommends a method of exposition that explicitly acknowledges and frames opposing arguments, so that the reader understands both sides and is reminded of the tension inherent in divine truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith is not a work but a gift
rubrics_metrics.description: Boasting is excluded not by the law of works but by faith; faith is not within our power like deeds of the law, and it is given to us in another way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theological claims about justification should emphasize that faith is bestowed rather than merited, shaping how one presents doctrines of salvation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of grace versus law
rubrics_metrics.description: The law has not destroyed nature but instructed it; grace has not destroyed the law but made it act. Grace gives what it imposes; faith received at baptism is the source of the Christian life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In doctrinal exposition, highlight that grace activates moral capacity rather than abolishing moral instruction; moral transformation is a product of grace working within nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of balanced spiritual feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosophers inspired feelings of pure greatness or pure littleness, neither of which is man's state; Christianity requires humility from penitence (not natural) and greatness from grace after humiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pastoral guidance and spiritual formation should cultivate a middle disposition that avoids both pride and despair and sequences humility before true greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The knowledge of God must be coupled with knowledge of human misery
rubrics_metrics.description: The knowledge of God without that of man's misery causes pride; the knowledge of man's misery without that of God causes despair; the knowledge of Jesus Christ constitutes the middle course because in Him we find both God and our misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any effective catechesis or apologetic must present both elements together to produce a rightly ordered spiritual state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing true disciples
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a great difference between disciples and true disciples: true disciples are recognised because 'the truth will make them free'; those who answer that they are already free are disciples but not true disciples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of spiritual authenticity should look for acknowledgement of bondage to sin and for openness to truth that brings freedom, not merely verbal claims of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical conduct: compare oneself with Christ, not others
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare not thyself with others, but with Me (Christ). If you compare yourself with those who do not have Christ, you compare to the abominable; compare yourself to Christ in you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and spiritual evaluation is to be Christ-centered rather than relative to other persons; spiritual progress measured by conformity to Christ avoids false complacency or despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of correction and mortification by fault-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: We owe a great debt to those who point out faults; they mortify us and prepare us for correction and freedom from fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communal or pastoral critique should be framed as corrective and formative; being open to reproach is a virtue in spiritual growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of metaphysical proofs alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The metaphysical proofs of God are remote and make little impression; knowledge of God obtained without Jesus Christ is communion without a mediator and often leads to self-glorification rather than salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apologetics should not rely solely on abstract metaphysical demonstration but incorporate historical, scriptural, and Christ-centered proofs (prophecy, fulfillment, and mediation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of prophetic testimony (custody, zeal, and rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: God chose a carnal people to hold the prophecies so that their zeal and custody of the books would make the testimony unusually trustworthy; their subsequent rejection of Christ serves as additional proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical-sociological considerations (who preserved the texts and how they treated the purported Messiah) as part of the evidential case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual practice: interior speech and silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Man holds an inward talk with himself which he must regulate well: 'Corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava.' Keep silent as much as possible and talk with ourselves only of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal discipline for moral formation includes regulating internal dialogue, practicing silence, and directing thoughts toward God as a means of conviction and truth-formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral lesson from Christ’s agony: vigilance and prayer
rubrics_metrics.description: Jesus was left alone in His agony, found His friends asleep, and prayed; 'the spirit is willing and the flesh weak.' We must not sleep, must pray longer, and watch against indifference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spiritual guidance and liturgical formation should emphasize perseverance in prayer and vigilance, learning from Christ's example of solitary suffering and reliance on the Father.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theodicy and teleology: the world ordered to instruct about God and redemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole course of things tends to establish the two chief points of religion: Jesus Christ is the end of all and the centre to which all tends; the order of the world and human sentiments should point to these truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apologetic interpretation of history and nature should read teleology: events and dispositions are intelligible as oriented toward the revelation in Christ, not merely as neutral data.
